notes.h: Skill, technique and a skilled performance
points: Skill: a learned ability to bring about a predetermined result with maximum certainty and the minimum outlay of time and/or energy. Barbara Knapp (1963) defined it as the learned ability to bring about pre-determined results with maximum certainty, often with the minimum outlay of time or energy or both.
A skill is learned through practice and is goal-directed: the performer knows the result they want before they start.

Technique: the way a skill is executed, meaning the specific movement pattern used. Two players can both have the skill of a basketball free throw but use different techniques, such as a one-handed or two-handed release.

The specification defines a skilled performance as one in which a sequence of movements is performed in a fluent and controlled manner, the right options are selected, and the skills and techniques used fully reflect the performer's ability and experience.
A skilled performance therefore includes decision-making, not only movement quality: a perfectly struck pass to a marked team-mate is not a skilled performance.

notes.b: Each characteristic can be seen in a named skill such as the basketball jump shot, the Gaelic football solo or the tennis serve.
points: Consistent: the outcome can be repeated reliably, even under pressure late in a match; a skilled free-taker scores from similar positions again and again.
Accurate and precise: the intended outcome is achieved, such as a tennis serve landing in the chosen corner of the service box.
Fluent and well co-ordinated: movements flow smoothly from one phase to the next with good timing, such as the run-up, gather and release of a jump shot.
Controlled: the performer is in control of the body and any implement throughout, such as keeping the ball close while soloing at speed.
Efficient: no wasted movement or energy is used (economy of movement, covered fully in the notes on movement and quality perspectives).
Aesthetically pleasing: the movement looks good to an observer, which matters most in judged activities such as gymnastics and dance.
Adaptable: the right option is chosen and the skill is adjusted to the situation, using anticipation and reading of the play, such as switching from a shot to a pass when a defender closes in.
Learned and goal-directed: the movement results from practice and has a clear intended outcome.
A novice shows the opposite features: movements are jerky and inconsistent, errors are frequent, and decisions are slow or wrong.
Ability: an inherited (innate), stable and enduring trait that a person brings to the learning of skills.
Abilities underpin skills and set a person's potential in an activity.

Edwin Fleishman classified motor abilities into two groups: perceptual-motor abilities, such as reaction time, co-ordination, balance and spatial awareness, and physical proficiency abilities, such as strength, flexibility and stamina.
Each skill draws on several abilities: a tennis serve needs co-ordination, timing, power and flexibility.
One ability supports many skills: good hand-eye co-ordination helps with catching, striking a sliotar and returning a serve.

notes.h: The difference between skill and ability
points: Origin: skill is learned; ability is largely inherited.
Change: skill can develop quickly with practice; ability is relatively stable and changes only slowly, influenced by genetics and early development.
Relationship: skills are built on abilities, and ability decides how quickly and how far a skill can be developed.
Example: a young basketball player with excellent co-ordination and speed (abilities) still has to practise to develop a reliable lay-up (skill).
Natural ability alone is not enough to succeed: without practice, coaching, feedback and psychological preparation, ability is never turned into a skilled performance.
A less gifted performer who practises well and is well coached can outperform a more gifted performer who does not.

notes.b: Most skills sit somewhere between the two extremes of each type, so each is a continuum. The types decide which practice methods suit a skill.
points: Open skill: performed in an unpredictable environment that the performer must react to, and usually externally paced, such as passing in a game.
Closed skill: performed in a stable, predictable environment, usually self-paced, such as a basketball free throw or a gymnastics vault.
Discrete skill: has a clear beginning and end, such as a penalty kick.
Serial skill: a series of discrete elements linked in order, such as the hop, step and jump of a triple jump.
Continuous skill: has no clear beginning or end, and each movement cycle runs into the next, such as running or swimming.
Gross skill: uses large muscle groups and whole-body movement, such as a shot-put.
Fine skill: uses small muscle groups for precise, delicate movement, such as a snooker shot or a dart throw.
Self-paced skill: the performer decides when to start and how fast to go, such as a tennis serve.
Externally paced skill: the timing is set by the environment or opponents, such as receiving a serve.

notes.h: Applying skills to a named activity: basketball
points: Jump shot: scores points from mid-range and over a defender, so the team can score when the defence is set.
Bounce pass: keeps possession by passing below a defender's reach to a team-mate cutting to the basket.
Defensive slide: lets a defender stay between the attacker and the basket without crossing the feet, preventing penetration.

factCards.definition: The learned ability to bring about pre-determined results with maximum certainty, often with the minimum outlay of time or energy or both.
Skill is learned, ability is largely inherited; skill develops quickly with practice, ability is relatively stable; skills are built on several abilities.

factCards.term: Fleishman's two groups of motor ability
factCards.definition: Perceptual-motor abilities (e.g. reaction time, co-ordination, balance) and physical proficiency abilities (e.g. strength, flexibility, stamina).

factCards.term: Four characteristics of a skilled performance
factCards.definition: Any four of: consistent, accurate, fluent and co-ordinated, controlled, efficient, aesthetically pleasing, adaptable with correct decisions, learned and goal-directed.

factCards.term: Can a performer succeed with natural ability alone?
factCards.definition: No: ability must be developed into skill through practice, coaching, feedback and psychological preparation.

questions.prompt: Identify and explain four characteristics of a skilled performance in a named physical activity.
questions.model: Activity: basketball, the jump shot. 1. Consistency: a skilled shooter scores from the same range again and again, including late in the game when tired and under pressure, because the movement pattern is grooved. 2. Fluency: the catch, gather, jump and release flow into one smooth action with no pause, so the shot is released before the defender can close. 3. Efficiency: no energy is wasted on unnecessary movement, such as an exaggerated dip of the ball, so the shooter can repeat the shot throughout a match. 4. Correct decision-making: the skilled player recognises when the defender is too close and passes or drives instead of forcing the shot.

questions.prompt: Discuss the difference between skill and ability, using examples from physical activity.
questions.model: Ability is an inherited, stable and enduring trait, such as reaction time, co-ordination or strength, that a person brings to learning. Skill is learned through practice and is the ability to bring about a predetermined result with maximum certainty and minimum time or energy. Skill can be developed quickly with good practice, whereas ability changes only slowly. Skills are built on abilities: the tennis serve depends on co-ordination, timing, power and flexibility, and a player with good co-ordination will usually learn it faster. However, ability sets potential only; a player with excellent hand-eye co-ordination still has to practise the ball toss, racket path and contact point to develop a consistent, accurate serve. One ability can also support many skills, so good co-ordination helps both catching and striking.

questions.prompt: Can a performer succeed with natural ability alone? Explain your answer.
questions.model: No. Natural ability, such as speed or co-ordination, is inherited and sets a performer's potential, but skills are learned. Without practice the performer will not develop consistent, accurate technique; without coaching and feedback they will not correct errors; and without psychological preparation they may not perform under pressure. For example, a fast young Gaelic footballer who does not practise kicking off both feet will be easy to mark, while a less gifted team-mate who practises well may become the more skilled player.
